rationale:
This slate is built around EASD 2026 news from 29–30 Sep, and every piece stays within the GLP-1 focus. The long-form is the EloraTZP headline decoder. It has the highest radar momentum and low competition, and the 'Did X really beat Y?' format beat our median. S1 is a spin-off of L1 that explains amylin, so it drives traffic to the long video.

S2 (GLP-1 nails) and S3 (orforglipron heart safety) are both emerging stories with low competition. They use search-style questions with a drug name people know.

The carousels cover two different topics. C1 refreshes the evergreen alcohol and reward-system question with new trial coverage, and its 'not approved for this' framing makes it the myth-busting piece. C2 is a cost and adherence checklist built on the new JAMA Health Forum data. It only lists legitimate ways to lower cost.

Mix: 4 emerging (L1, S1, S2, S3), 1 evergreen with a timely hook (C2), and 1 myth-bust (C1).

Body systems are spread out: digestive and hormone (L1, S1), skin and nails (S2), heart (S3), brain and reward (C1), and behaviour and cost (C2). No pillar is used more than twice.

Skipped and why:
- Retatrutide decoder: we did a long-form on 09-30.
- Zepbound vs Wegovy HD: we did a carousel on 09-30.
- GI side-effect habits: we did a carousel on 09-30.
- Non-responder topic: we did a carousel on 09-29.
- Trevogrumab: it overlaps the 09-28 muscle framework too much.
- Novo's MACE switching claim: it would read as switching advice.
- Paediatric deficiency: it's outside our adult audience.
- Wegovy pill switch: the same switching risk. We hold it for a later, careful slot.

pieces.topic: EloraTZP (eloralintide + tirzepatide) vs tirzepatide 15 mg in adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes: phase 2b, 367 adults, 48 weeks, EASD 2026
pieces.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide + Amylin (EloraTZP) vs Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) in Type 2 Diabetes: 23.3% vs 14.8% in Phase 2' (fits the ≤100 character limit). In the first 10 seconds say: top dose, 48 weeks, adults with T2D plus overweight or obesity, small Phase 2b, numerical comparison not formally tested, more people stopped the combo because of side effects. Include placebo figures, show the arm sizes, and set the discontinuation rates side by side from the primary source. Status: investigational, Phase 3 planned (Lilly says by end of 2026). Nothing changes for people on tirzepatide today. End with the exact prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Did Lilly's New Combo Beat Tirzepatide (Mounjaro)? EloraTZP's 23.3% vs 14.8% Explained
pieces.why: Top radar momentum (88), low competition, and it's brand-new: there are almost no consumer explainers yet. It fits the headline-decoder format that beat our median, and phase 2b data gives enough depth for 10+ minutes. | fact-check: Core numbers check out against Lilly's EASD 2026 release and the HCPLive write-up. The trial was 48 weeks, 367 adults with obesity or overweight AND type 2 diabetes, run in the US and Argentina, double-blind and placebo-controlled. It had placebo, eloralintide-alone, tirzepatide 15 mg and EloraTZP arms. Baseline was 105.4 kg and A1C 8.1% (≈65 mmol/mol). EloraTZP gave 13.2–23.3% weight loss (23.3% at the top dose) vs 14.8% with tirzepatide 15 mg. Eloralintide alone gave 8.2–12.3%. A1C fell by 2.2–2.9 percentage points vs 2.4 with tirzepatide. Lilly plans Phase 3 of an optimised co-formulation by the end of 2026. Problems to fix: (1) The working title has no population and no 'top dose' / Phase 2 qualifier. It also says 'beat' when no p-values for EloraTZP vs tirzepatide were reported, so they are numerical comparisons, not proven superiority. (2) Dropout rates are a major limit and must be shown with their comparator. HCPLive reports adverse-event discontinuation of 10.8–27.0% for EloraTZP vs 2.9% for tirzepatide (placebo is listed as 16.7%, which looks odd). Take these only from Lilly's primary release or the EASD abstract, and check whether each figure is 'due to adverse events' or overall. (3) With 367 people split across many arms, each arm is roughly 30–40 people. Say this. (4) Report placebo weight loss next to the drug figures, and name the estimand (efficacy vs treatment-regimen) as the primary source does. (5) Never refer to the 'tirzepatide 15 mg' arm as dosing guidance. Phrase it as 'the highest approved tirzepatide dose arm' and don't give titration detail. Amylin context: CagriSema (Novo), petrelintide (Zealand/Roche) and EloraTZP are all investigational as of Sept 2026. Pramlintide is an older approved amylin analogue used with insulin; say so if you claim 'no amylin drug is approved', or avoid that claim.

pieces.topic: What is amylin? The 'second fullness hormone' behind the new combo weight-loss drugs
pieces.angle: One sharp idea: GLP-1 isn't the only gut and pancreas fullness signal. Amylin is released with insulin after meals. It slows stomach emptying and signals 'full' to the brain. That's why the newest drugs pair it with GLP-1 (CagriSema, EloraTZP), or try it alone (petrelintide). Use one verified number from L1 with its arm and population: 'up to 23.3%, top dose, adults with T2D, phase 2b, 48 weeks'. Say on screen: 'investigational, not approved as of Sept 2026'. Point viewers to the full video. Add the exact prescriber line. Aim for 35–50s.
pieces.working_title: What Is Amylin? The Hormone Behind Lilly's New Combo With Tirzepatide #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1. It answers the search question that today's headlines raise and sends viewers to the long video. It also tests a 35–50s cut.

pieces.topic: GLP-1 users and nail detachment (onycholysis): 39% vs 9% in comparable non-users, the first controlled study (575 users vs 1,329 controls, EADV 2026)
pieces.angle: Title: 'Can GLP-1 Drugs Like Ozempic Affect Your Nails? 39% vs 9% Self-Reported #shorts'. Answer within 10 seconds: 'A new survey-style study found more nail problems in people taking GLP-1s, but it can't show the drug causes them.' On screen: '575 GLP-1 users vs 1,329 non-users with T2D/obesity · self-reported · cross-sectional · congress abstract, not peer-reviewed · ~2–3× after adjustment'. Add a one-line definition of onycholysis, gentle nail-care habits with no supplement claims, when to see a clinician, and the exact prescriber line. Don't tell anyone to stop their medicine.
pieces.working_title: Can Ozempic (Semaglutide) Affect Your Nails? 39% vs 9% in First Controlled Study #shorts
pieces.why: A brand-new controlled number on a complaint that already circulates on Reddit and TikTok. Creators haven't covered it yet, and it extends our hair-loss piece (top 2 of 5 long-forms). | fact-check: Verified: EADV Congress 2026, 575 GLP-1 RA users vs 1,329 people with T2D and/or obesity who had never used them, recruited in France, the US, Brazil and Mexico. Nail detachment was 39% vs 9% and discoloration 46% vs 17%. The study was cross-sectional, with patient-reported symptoms, and is a congress abstract that hasn't been peer-reviewed. After adjustment the gap shrank to about 2–3× more frequent. The authors say it cannot establish causation. Problems: (1) The title leads with Ozempic/semaglutide, but the study covered GLP-1 RA users in general, and the specific drugs aren't reported. This breaks the brand rule. (2) 'First controlled study' is the press-release framing. Say 'described by researchers as the first controlled study', or drop it. (3) The raw 39% vs 9% must sit next to 'about 2–3× after adjustment'. Don't use the press 'over 4x higher risk' wording. These are self-reported prevalence figures, not risk. (4) Don't imply that protein prevents nail changes. Habits are general nail care and a balanced diet, not a fix. Add the red flags: pain, signs of infection, or changes in only one nail mean see a GP or dermatologist. Keep the tone reassuring, not alarming.

pieces.topic: Orforglipron (Foundayo) pill passes its heart-safety test vs insulin glargine in type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk (ACHIEVE-4, The Lancet)
pieces.angle: Title: 'Is the Orforglipron (Foundayo) Pill Safe for the Heart? ACHIEVE-4 vs Insulin Glargine #shorts'. Answer: 'In about 2,700 adults with type 2 diabetes plus overweight or obesity at higher heart risk, followed for about 2 years, it was not worse than insulin glargine for major heart events: 4.2% vs 5.0%, HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.59–1.20.' Explain that non-inferior means 'not worse', not 'proven better'. The death signal (HR 0.43) is nominal, so a hint, not proof. Limits: open-label, compared with insulin rather than placebo, Lilly-funded. Approval status hedged as of Sept 2026. Exact prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Is the Orforglipron (Foundayo) Pill Safe for Your Heart? ACHIEVE-4 vs Insulin #shorts
pieces.why: Published in the Lancet on 30 Sep and hasn't reached consumers yet. Foundayo is a newly searched brand, and our orforglipron long-form had the top views. It also does evidence literacy (non-inferior ≠ better), which covers the myth-busting share. | fact-check: Verified: ACHIEVE-4 was published in The Lancet (2026). It was open-label, non-inferiority and active-comparator (insulin glargine), with 2,749 randomised: 1,371 to orforglipron and 1,378 to glargine. Median follow-up was about 2 years. MACE-4 occurred in 57/1,358 (4.2%) vs 67/1,343 (5.0%), HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.59–1.20), and non-inferiority was met. All-cause death HR was 0.43 (95% CI 0.25–0.75), nominal P=.002, so it's hypothesis-generating. Fixes: (1) The population is adults with T2D AND overweight or obesity at increased cardiovascular risk. Add 'overweight or obesity'. (2) Use the analysed n from the Lancet paper (1,358 + 1,343 in the primary analysis) and say which n you're using. (3) MACE-4 includes hospitalisation for unstable angina, so define it, not just 'heart attack and stroke'. (4) Foundayo approval status: US approval for obesity in April 2026 and UK in August 2026 per the coverage. Don't imply it is approved for T2D unless you confirm that, and hedge with 'as of Sept 2026'. (5) Generic name first. Foundayo is orforglipron's brand, so using it is OK for recognition. (6) Put the absolute rates (4.2% vs 5.0%) next to the HR.

pieces.topic: Does Ozempic curb alcohol cravings? What the semaglutide trials in alcohol use disorder actually show
pieces.angle: Title: 'Does Semaglutide (Ozempic) Curb Alcohol Cravings? What 3 Trials in Alcohol Use Disorder Show'. Slide order: question → mechanism → Lancet 2026 RCT (AUD + obesity, 26 weeks) → JAMA Psychiatry 2025 (9 weeks, small, low dose) → AJP 2026 oral trial (8 weeks, n=50) → mouse data labelled 'in mice' → what we don't know (not approved for AUD, short trials, mostly small, people with obesity in the largest trial) → where to get help (SAMHSA, GP/NHS, Drinkline, plus a warning that heavy drinkers shouldn't stop abruptly without medical advice) → questions for your clinician. Source tag on every slide, no doses, exact prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Does Ozempic (Semaglutide) Curb Alcohol Cravings? What 2 Small Trials Show
pieces.why: A rising brain and reward story with fresh coverage, and Q4 'Dry January' interest is building. The careful 'promising, not approved for this' framing makes it today's myth-busting piece, and it adds a body system no other piece covers. | fact-check: The evidence has moved on, so '2 small trials' is now out of date and would mislead viewers. Verified so far: (a) Hendershot et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2025: low-dose weekly semaglutide vs placebo for 9 weeks in about 48 adults with AUD who weren't seeking treatment. It reduced heavy-drinking days (primary endpoint in the published paper; confirm the endpoint wording) and craving. (b) CU Anschutz oral semaglutide RCT, American Journal of Psychiatry 2026: 50 treatment-seeking adults with moderate to severe AUD, 8 weeks. It reduced heavy-drinking days, drinking intensity, craving and consequences. (c) The Lancet 2026: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT of once-weekly semaglutide in AUD with comorbid obesity, reporting fewer heavy-drinking days at 26 weeks. This is the largest and strongest trial so it must go first, following the 'strongest evidence first' rule. Pull exact n, duration and effect sizes from each paper. Don't use any dosing detail (e.g. 3 mg → 7 mg) on slides; that breaks the no-dosing rule. Keep observational data such as the Healio Aug 2026 item labelled 'linked to'. 'Curb cravings' in the title is fine because craving was a measured outcome, but say 'in adults with alcohol use disorder'. Semaglutide is not approved for AUD anywhere as of Sept 2026. The help slide is good. SAMHSA's helpline 1-800-662-4357 is correct. For the UK, add 'your GP, or Drinkline 0300 123 1110'. Add a note that people should not stop alcohol abruptly without medical advice if they drink heavily, because withdrawal can be dangerous.

pieces.topic: Cost and sticking with a GLP-1: non-adherence rose above 80% once out-of-pocket costs passed $75 a month (UGA, JAMA Health Forum, 8,914 insured adults)
pieces.angle: Title: 'Why People Miss GLP-1 Doses: What Happens Above $75 a Month, and 5 Legit Cost Questions (US)'. Slide 1: 'Observational study of 8,914 insured US adults: adjusted non-adherence was about 75–77% up to $75/month, 79.7% at $76–168, and 85.2% above $168', with the paper's exact definition of non-adherence. Then: why it matters (no 'don't stop' guilt) → insurer questions (coverage, prior authorization, appeals) → official manufacturer savings and direct-pay programmes with their limits → Medicare rules verified on CMS 'as of Sept 2026' → questions for your prescriber or pharmacist (covered alternatives, never change your dose to stretch supply) → warning against compounded, gray-market and research products. US-only label, source tag on every slide, exact prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: Why People Stop GLP-1s: The $75 Cost Tipping Point and 5 Legit Questions to Ask
pieces.why: An evergreen cost and access worry refreshed by new JAMA Health Forum data. A save-and-share checklist fits the carousel format, and it pushes viewers away from unsafe sources, in line with the brand guardrails. | fact-check: Verified (UGA Today, JAMA Health Forum 2026): 8,914 continuously insured US adults who started GLP-1s for weight loss over a 1.5-year study period. The study is observational (claims-based). Out-of-pocket bands were $0–21, $22–43, $44–75, $76–168 and >$168. Adjusted non-adherence was 74.7–76.6% across the 3 cheapest bands, 79.7% at $76–168 and 85.2% above $168. Problems: (1) 'Above 80% once costs passed $75' is press-release framing. The $76–168 band was 79.7% adjusted, so use the paper's adjusted band figures, not 'rose above 80%'. (2) 'About 3 in 4 stopped within a year' may confuse non-adherence (probably a proportion-of-days-covered threshold, i.e. missing doses) with stopping. Use the paper's exact definition and don't say 'stopped' unless the paper does. (3) Confirm which GLP-1s were included (one write-up says semaglutide) and the insurance type (commercial?). (4) Medicare: anti-obesity GLP-1 coverage and the $50 cap programme are changing in 2026. Verify the exact eligibility and dates against CMS/Medicare.gov, hedge with 'as of Sept 2026', and don't imply all Medicare enrollees qualify. (5) Manufacturer savings and direct-pay programmes are fine if they come from the official manufacturer site, with their limits stated (commercial insurance only; usually not valid with government insurance). Keep the warning against compounded, gray-market and 'research' products, and the 'don't stop or change your dose to save money without talking to your prescriber' line.
